title: Central chest pain in a 50-year-old man
desc: This station involves a focused chest pain history and examination of a 50-year-old man brought to the ED by ambulance, who becomes bradycardic and hypotensive during the history. The candidate then interprets his observations, 12-lead ECG and bloods, recognises an inferior STEMI, and outlines reperfusion, immediate management, secondary prevention and safety netting.
focus: Acute chest pain: a focused history, recognising an inferior STEMI on the ECG, and immediate reperfusion and secondary prevention
stem: You are the junior doctor in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital that has a cardiac catheter laboratory. James, a 50-year-old civil engineer, has been brought in by ambulance from work with chest pain. The crew were a non-emergency transport crew who were nearby, so no 12-lead ECG was done and no medicines were given. He is on a trolley in the acute area and a nurse has put in an IV cannula. The nurse is with you and will carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from James and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Act on anything the nurse tells you (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you James's observations, his 12-lead ECG and his blood results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are James, a 50-year-old civil engineer. The ambulance brought you in from work. You sit up on the trolley, pale and sweaty, rubbing the middle of your chest. You are in pain but can talk in full sentences. A nurse is with the candidate and does what they ask. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

Opening line: "I've got this awful pressure in my chest. It's like an elephant sitting on me."

History (give only when asked)

The pain

  • Site: the middle of your chest.
  • Onset: about an hour ago, while you were sitting at your desk at work.
  • Character: a heavy pressure, "like an elephant sitting on my chest".
  • Radiation: up into the left jaw.
  • Time course: constant for the whole hour, and it has got a bit worse.
  • Exacerbating and relieving factors: nothing makes it better or worse. You chewed a couple of antacid tablets at work and they made no difference. Breathing, moving and changing position do not change it.
  • Severity: 7/10.
  • You have never had pain like this before.

Associated symptoms

  • Yes: you are sweaty, you feel sick (no vomiting) and you are a little short of breath.
  • No palpitations. No fainting (until the nurse's report below).

Other causes (all negative, give only if asked)

  • Heart failure: no breathlessness lying flat, no waking up gasping at night, no ankle swelling.
  • Pericarditis: no recent cold or flu. The pain is not sharp and is no better leaning forward.
  • Aortic dissection: the pain is not tearing or ripping, did not come on at full strength in an instant, and does not go to your back or abdomen.
  • Clots: no long trips, no time off your feet, no recent operation, no cancer, no calf pain or swelling.
  • Lungs: the pain is no worse when you breathe in, and the breathlessness did not come on suddenly.
  • Gut: no acid taste or burning with this pain, no vomiting blood. You get heartburn now and then after a big meal, but it feels nothing like this.

Risk factors

  • Smoking: never.
  • High cholesterol: yes. Your GP told you a few years ago and said to watch your diet. You do not take tablets for it.
  • Diabetes: no.
  • High blood pressure: yes.
  • Family history of heart disease: yes (see below).

Past medical history

  • High blood pressure and high cholesterol.
  • Tonsils out at 8 years old. No other hospital stays. Generally pretty healthy. Immunisations up to date.
  • No previous heart problems and no stress tests.

Bleeding and medicine safety (only if asked)

  • No bleeding problems, no stroke, no recent operation or injury, no stomach ulcers.
  • No blood thinners. No tablets for erections (such as Viagra).

Medications and allergies

  • Amlodipine 5 mg daily.
  • Panadol now and then, and antacids.
  • No vitamins or supplements. No recreational drugs, ever.
  • No allergies.

Family history

  • Mother: heart attack at 50, now has heart failure.
  • Father: mild osteoarthritis and high cholesterol.
  • Brother: has angina, diagnosed at 45.

Social history

  • Non-smoker. 1 to 2 beers socially on weekends.
  • Civil engineer.
  • Exercises regularly and plays community futsal.
  • Eats well. Your wife cooks at home.
  • You live with your wife and your 1-year-old son. You have a close circle of friends.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: "Could it be indigestion?" You are worried about missing work because you are in the middle of a big project. You were hoping for something for indigestion so you can get back to work.

  • Around minute 3, whether or not the candidate has asked, say: "It's just indigestion, isn't it? I need to get back to work."

The nurse and how James changes

  • When asked, the nurse gives the arrival observations (13:10): HR 60 regular, BP 132/84, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, BGL 7.2 mmol/L. The crew were a non-emergency transport crew who were nearby; no 12-lead was done and no medicines were given.
  • If the candidate asks for an ECG, the nurse says it was recorded at 13:15 and the examiner will give it in Part 2. Bloods were sent from the cannula at 13:20.
  • If the candidate orders a medicine, calls a senior or asks for anything else, the nurse says "Will do." The examiner notes it for marking in Part 2.
  • About 7 minutes into Part 1 (or when the examination starts if it is sooner), the nurse says: "Doctor, his heart rate has dropped to 46 on the monitor and his blood pressure is 96 over 60." James says: "I feel a bit faint and sick."
  • If the candidate lies James flat, he feels a little less faint but stays pale and clammy. Repeat observations are on the chart given in Part 2.

Exam findings

  • General: anxious, pale and sweaty, in pain, speaking in full sentences. No xanthelasma.
  • Pulses: radial pulse 60 and regular (46 after the nurse's report). The radial pulses are equal, with no radio-radial delay. The femoral pulses are equal.
  • Blood pressure: right arm 132/84, left arm 128/82 (96/60 after the nurse's report).
  • Perfusion: warm peripheries, CRT 2 seconds. After the nurse's report: cool and clammy, CRT 3 seconds.
  • JVP: not raised, 3 cm above the sternal angle. After the nurse's report: JVP 5 cm above the sternal angle, lungs still clear.
  • Heart: dual heart sounds, no murmurs, no pericardial rub.
  • Chest wall: not tender.
  • Lungs: equal expansion, resonant to percussion, vesicular breath sounds, no crackles or wheeze.
  • Abdomen: soft and non-tender, no epigastric tenderness, no pulsatile mass.
  • Legs: calves soft and non-tender, no swelling, no pitting oedema.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self, confirms James's identity and explains what they are doing while he is in pain.

Recognises a possible acute coronary syndrome from the start: straight away asks the nurse for the observations, continuous cardiac monitoring and a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival, and keeps the history focused.

Uses plain language and empathy. Acknowledges his pain and responds to his questions about indigestion and missing work without dismissing them; or, in Part 2, explains in plain words that this is a heart attack needing an urgent procedure and offers to call his wife.
History
Characterises the chest pain:

kids.x: Site and character: central, a heavy pressure ('like an elephant sitting on my chest')
Onset and time course: started about an hour ago at rest, constant and getting a bit worse
Severity 7/10, and that nothing changes it (antacids, breathing, position)

check.x: Asks about associated symptoms of myocardial infarction: sweating, nausea or vomiting, breathlessness, palpitations, light-headedness and syncope.
Asks cluster questions for the other causes of chest pain:

kids.x: Aortic dissection: sudden tearing pain at full strength from the start, radiating to the back or abdomen
Pulmonary embolism and pneumothorax: immobility, recent surgery, cancer, calf pain or swelling, sudden breathlessness, pleuritic pain
Pericarditis: viral prodrome, sharp pain, better leaning forward
Heart failure: orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, ankle swelling
Oesophagitis or GORD: reflux, epigastric burning, blood-streaked vomit

check.x: Asks specifically about cardiac risk factors: smoking (never), cholesterol (high, untreated), diabetes (no) and hypertension (yes); family history is credited in item 10.
Takes a family history: mother had a heart attack at 50 and now has heart failure, brother has angina from age 45, father has high cholesterol and osteoarthritis.

Takes the past history, medications and allergies: hypertension, high cholesterol, tonsillectomy at 8, no previous cardiac symptoms; amlodipine 5 mg daily, occasional paracetamol and antacids, no anticoagulants, no PDE5 inhibitor; no allergies.
Checks for contraindications to antithrombotic and fibrinolytic therapy: bleeding problems, previous stroke, recent surgery or trauma, peptic ulcer.
Takes a focused social history, credited for alcohol, recreational drugs (including cocaine) and any two of occupation, exercise, diet, home and supports.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: he thinks it is indigestion and is worried about missing work.
Examination
General inspection (pale, sweaty, distressed) and reviews the vital signs: HR, BP, RR, SpO2, temperature and BGL.
Compares the radial pulses and the BP in both arms (and the femoral pulses), looking for the asymmetry of aortic dissection.
Cardiovascular examination: perfusion (CRT, peripheral temperature), JVP, heart sounds, any new murmur (mitral or aortic regurgitation) and a pericardial rub.
Respiratory examination: expansion, percussion and auscultation, listening for the crackles of heart failure and the reduced breath sounds of a pneumothorax.
Palpates the chest wall and abdomen (epigastric tenderness, pulsatile mass) and examines the calves for DVT.

Responds to the nurse's report of HR 46 and BP 96/60: reassesses James at once (ABC, perfusion), calls a senior, and asks for defibrillator pads; also credit lying him flat, a repeat ECG or rhythm strip, or preparing atropine.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: all white zone on arrival, then at 13:20 HR 46 and systolic BP 96 are both in the yellow zone (clinical review, or a rapid response call per local escalation policy), with a worried nurse, so the senior comes now.
Identifies about 2 mm ST elevation in the contiguous inferior leads II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL as an inferior STEMI.
Reports the ECG systematically, with its time (13:15), rate (60/min) and rhythm (sinus), PR, QRS and QTc.

Names the right coronary artery as the likely culprit (left circumflex in a left-dominant circulation) and links it to the bradycardia and hypotension (AV nodal ischaemia, right ventricular involvement).
States the raised hs-troponin T (38 ng/L) shows myocardial injury, but the reperfusion decision rests on the ECG and does not wait for the troponin or a repeat.

Gives inferior STEMI as the most likely diagnosis and considers aortic dissection involving the right coronary artery, with a feature against it (gradual pressure-like pain, no tearing or back pain, equal arm BPs and pulses, no AR murmur).
Justifies the other differentials, each with a feature against it: pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, and GORD or oesophageal spasm.
Management

Gets the senior ED doctor to the bedside and activates the STEMI pathway (cath lab activation via the interventional cardiologist or cardiology registrar per local protocol) for primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact, then coronary care unit admission.
Gives aspirin 300 mg chewed or dispersed, with a P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or prasugrel preferred, clopidogrel acceptable) and heparin as the interventional cardiologist directs.
Withholds GTN because of inferior STEMI with bradycardia and hypotension (possible RV infarction), and requests right-sided leads (V4R).

Manages the bradycardia and hypotension: IV atropine 500–600 microgram (repeat to max 3 mg) if bradycardia with hypotension or poor perfusion persists, cautious IV fluid bolus (e.g. 250 mL) for suspected RV infarction, transcutaneous pacing if refractory.

Gives small, titrated IV opioid doses (fentanyl preferred over morphine given the hypotension and bradycardia; morphine delays oral P2Y12 absorption) with an antiemetic, watching the BP. Oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 93%, so none at 97%.
Secondary prevention and safety netting

Outlines secondary prevention: aspirin long term plus a P2Y12 inhibitor for 12 months, a high-intensity statin (LDL 4.5 untreated), a beta blocker once the bradycardia settles, an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) with a plan for his amlodipine, and GTN.

Tells James the warning signs in plain words with a GTN action plan. For chest pain, stop and use GTN, and call 000 if the pain is severe, getting worse or lasts 10 minutes. Also report breathlessness, fainting, palpitations, bleeding, or swelling at the catheter site.

part2.lead: Here are James's observations from arrival, his 12-lead ECG and his blood results.
part2.patient:
When the candidate explains what is happening, ask:

  • "So it's not indigestion?"
  • "I've got a big project on at work. When can I go back?"

You are frightened when you hear it is a heart attack, because your mother had one at your age. You settle if the candidate explains clearly, without jargon, and offers to call your wife.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Arrival set at 13:10; the nurse repeated the set at 13:20 when James said he felt faint. Monitor at 13:20: regular rhythm, 46/min. Any medicines ordered in Part 1 had not yet taken effect at 13:20.
handover.model:
• Read: at 13:10 every value is in the white zone: HR 60, BP 132/84, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, BGL 7.2. Pain is severe at 7/10. At 13:20 HR 46 and systolic BP 96 are both in the yellow zone, he is pale, clammy and light-headed, and the nurse is concerned.
  • Meaning: new bradycardia with hypotension in a man with ongoing ischaemic pain. With the inferior ECG changes this points to right coronary artery ischaemia of the AV node, or a vagal reflex, with or without right ventricular involvement.
  • Changes: two yellow zone values call at least for a clinical review (or a rapid response call per local escalation policy). In a STEMI with a worried nurse, the senior ED doctor comes to the bedside now. Lie him flat, put pads on and keep him on continuous monitoring. Get a rhythm strip and a repeat ECG to look for AV block. Do not give GTN.

rows.note: Arrived by ambulance from work; cardiac monitoring on
Pale, clammy, nauseated and light-headed; doctor informed

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, recorded 13:15 in the ED (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV). James, 50-year-old man, central chest pain.

  • Rate: 60/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus rhythm, regular, a P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal, about +60°.
  • P waves: normal morphology.
  • PR interval: 160 ms.
  • QRS: 90 ms. No pathological Q waves, no bundle branch block.
  • QTc: 420 ms.
  • ST segments: inferior leads II, III and aVF: ST elevation of about 2 mm, greatest in III. aVL: 1 mm ST depression. Lead I: 0.5 mm ST depression. V1 to V6: no ST elevation, and no ST depression in V1 to V3.
  • T waves: upright and broad in II, III and aVF, inverted in aVL.
  • U waves: none.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG available. Right-sided leads not recorded.
handover.model:
• Read: confirms the patient details and the time (13:15). Sinus rhythm at 60/min (rate normal, just), normal axis, normal P waves, PR 160 ms, narrow QRS, normal QTc. About 2 mm ST elevation in the contiguous inferior leads II, III and aVF, with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. No Q waves yet, no posterior changes in V1 to V3, no old ECG for comparison.
  • Meaning: with an hour of ischaemic pain this is an inferior STEMI. Elevation greatest in III, with depression in I and aVL, favours the right coronary artery over the left circumflex. That explains the later bradycardia and hypotension (the AV node supply, possible right ventricular infarction).
  • Changes: activate the STEMI pathway now, without waiting for the troponin. Record right-sided leads (V4R) and avoid nitrates until right ventricular infarction is excluded and the BP recovers. Repeat the ECG with any change in rhythm or pain.

handover.label: Bloods
handover.result: Collected 13:20 from the IV cannula, about 70 minutes after the pain began. Lipids non-fasting.
handover.model:
• Read: hs-troponin T 38 ng/L is above the reference limit: acute myocardial injury. Hb 152, platelets 262, INR 1.0 and APTT 30 are normal. Potassium 4.1, magnesium 0.86 and creatinine 86 (eGFR above 90) are normal. Glucose 7.4 is a stress level, within range. Lipase is normal. Total cholesterol 6.6, LDL 4.5 and triglycerides 2.6 are high and HDL 0.9 is low.
  • Meaning: the troponin fits the STEMI but is early. A normal value would not have excluded it, and the decision rests on the ECG. Nothing stops antiplatelets, heparin, fibrinolysis or contrast, and a normal potassium and magnesium lower the risk of arrhythmia. The lipids show his known, untreated hypercholesterolaemia.
  • Changes: go to the cath lab without waiting for a repeat troponin. Start a high-intensity statin, and recheck the lipids on treatment.

ask: You are now calling the cardiology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of James, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of James now, here in the emergency department.
Before James goes home, what medicines will he need long term, and what warning signs would you tell him about?
expect:
• Identify: self, ED junior doctor; James, 50, in the ED.
  • Situation: inferior STEMI, now bradycardic and hypotensive.
  • Background: 1 hour of central pressure to the left jaw, 7/10, with sweating and nausea. Hypertension on amlodipine, untreated high cholesterol, mother had an MI at 50, brother has angina from 45, non-smoker. No bleeding risk, no allergies.
  • Assessment: ECG at 13:15: sinus rhythm 60, 2 mm ST elevation in II, III and aVF, reciprocal depression in I and aVL: inferior STEMI, likely RCA. Arrival observations at 13:10 normal (white zone); at 13:20 HR 46 and BP 96/60 (yellow zone). hs-troponin T 38, raised, confirming myocardial injury, but the diagnosis rests on the ECG. Bleeding screen normal.
  • Recommendation: please accept him for primary PCI within 90 minutes, advise on the P2Y12 inhibitor and heparin, and help with the bradycardia.

Inferior STEMI, most likely from right coronary artery occlusion (left circumflex if left-dominant), which supplies the AV node and right ventricle, explaining the bradycardia and hypotension: an hour of central crushing pain to the jaw with sweating and nausea, strong risk factors, ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal change, raised troponin, and bradycardia with hypotension.

  • Aortic dissection involving the RCA (consider at the bedside before antithrombotics; image the aorta only if clinical features suggest it): for: hypertension. Against: gradual pressure, not tearing, no back pain, equal arm BPs and pulses, no aortic regurgitation murmur.
  • Pericarditis: against: no prodrome, not sharp or positional, no rub, territorial ST elevation with reciprocal change.
  • Pulmonary embolism: against: no risk factors, SpO2 97%, not pleuritic, normal calves.
  • GORD or oesophageal spasm: for: antacid use, his belief. Against: antacids did not help, jaw radiation, sweating, the ECG.

1. Senior ED doctor to the bedside. Continuous monitoring with pads on. Lie him flat.
  2. Activate the STEMI pathway now, on the ECG, without waiting for the troponin (cath lab activation via the interventional cardiologist or cardiology registrar per local protocol) for primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact. Then CCU.
  3. Aspirin 300 mg chewed. P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or prasugrel preferred, clopidogrel acceptable) and heparin as the cardiologist directs.
  4. No GTN (inferior STEMI with bradycardia and hypotension: possible RV infarction). Right-sided leads (V4R).
  5. Bradycardia with hypotension: IV atropine 500 microgram, repeated every 3–5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg, if it persists with hypotension or poor perfusion; a cautious crystalloid bolus (for example 250 mL, reassessing the chest) for suspected RV infarction; transcutaneous pacing if refractory.
  6. Small, titrated IV opioid doses (fentanyl preferred over morphine given the hypotension and bradycardia; morphine delays oral P2Y12 absorption) with an antiemetic, watching the BP. Oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 93%, so none at 97%.

• Medicines: aspirin long term plus a P2Y12 inhibitor for 12 months, a high-intensity statin, a beta blocker once the bradycardia has settled, an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) with a plan for his amlodipine, and a GTN spray.
  • Red flags: for chest pain, stop and use GTN, and call 000 if it is severe, getting worse or lasts 10 minutes; also breathlessness, fainting, palpitations, bleeding, or swelling at the wrist or groin.

ddx.dx: Inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (right coronary artery occlusion)
ddx.for: An hour of central crushing pain to the left jaw with sweating and nausea, hypertension, untreated high cholesterol and premature family history, ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL, a raised troponin, and new bradycardia with hypotension.

ddx.dx: Acute aortic dissection extending into the right coronary artery
ddx.for: He has hypertension and severe chest pain with inferior ST elevation, which a dissection can cause by occluding the right coronary ostium.
ddx.against: The pain came on gradually as a pressure, it is not tearing and does not go to the back, the arm BPs and pulses are equal, and there is no aortic regurgitation murmur.

ddx.for: He has chest pain with ST elevation.
ddx.against: No viral prodrome, the pain is pressure-like and not positional, there is no rub, and the ST elevation is territorial with reciprocal depression in aVL.

ddx.for: He has chest pain with mild breathlessness and has become hypotensive.
ddx.against: No immobility, surgery, cancer or calf symptoms, the pain is not pleuritic, SpO2 is 97% on room air and the calves are normal.

ddx.dx: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease or oesophageal spasm
ddx.for: He uses antacids for occasional heartburn, feels nauseated, and thinks this is indigestion.
ddx.against: Antacids did not help, the pain goes to the jaw with sweating, it feels nothing like his heartburn, and the ECG shows a STEMI.

guide:
GTN ordered in Part 1 before the 13:20 deterioration, with SBP above 90 and no PDE5 inhibitor, is not penalised. Item 33 is earned by stating in Part 2 that GTN is now withheld (or stopped) because of the bradycardia, hypotension and possible RV infarction; fail item 33 only if GTN is ordered or continued after the 13:20 observations. In Part 1, James answers the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they examine. The nurse gives the arrival observations when asked. Around minute 3 James asks whether it is just indigestion and says he needs to get back to work, so item 4 can be earned in Part 1 (or from his questions in Part 2). About 7 minutes in, or as the examination begins, the nurse reports HR 46 and BP 96/60 and James says he feels faint. Mark the bedside response (item 21) in Part 1. If the candidate asks for the ECG, the nurse says it was recorded at 13:15 and will be given in Part 2. This is an artefact of the format: in practice it would be read within 10 minutes of arrival. Treatment ordered in Part 1 (aspirin, analgesia, calling the cardiologist) is noted and credited against the Management items in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over the observations, ECG and bloods, then ask all four questions in order. Read out James's Part 2 questions only during question 4, and only if item 4 was not already earned in Part 1.

Credit naming the right coronary artery from either the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer. Accept ticagrelor, prasugrel or clopidogrel. The Australian threshold is primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact, otherwise fibrinolysis; also accept the ESC 120-minute threshold if the candidate names it as such. For oxygen, the Australian ACS guideline threshold is SpO2 below 93%; also accept below 90%, as long as the candidate does not give routine oxygen at 97%.

A high-performing candidate asks for the ECG and monitoring in the first minute, takes a SOCRATES history of the pain with associated symptoms, and screens with cluster questions for dissection, PE and pneumothorax, pericarditis, heart failure and oesophageal causes. They take the risk factors and family history and check bleeding risk. They compare the arm BPs and act at once when the nurse reports bradycardia. In Part 2 they read the ECG systematically, call it an inferior STEMI from the right coronary artery, and do not wait for the troponin. They activate the cath lab, give aspirin and withhold GTN because of the hypotension and possible right ventricular involvement. They know that primary PCI should happen within 90 minutes of first medical contact, with fibrinolysis if it cannot, and list secondary prevention, including an ACE inhibitor with a plan for his amlodipine.

A borderline candidate takes a long, unfocused history, does not ask about dissection or bleeding risk, or ignores the nurse's report. They describe the ECG as "ST changes" without a territory, wait for the troponin or call for "cardiology review" without activating reperfusion, give GTN despite the hypotension, or give vague safety netting.

Allow about 90 seconds for the ISBAR, 75 seconds each for the diagnosis and management, and 60 seconds for the fourth question.
explain:
Diagnosis: inferior STEMI

James has an hour of central, heavy chest pain radiating to the left jaw, with sweating, nausea and breathlessness. He has hypertension, untreated hypercholesterolaemia and a strong family history of premature coronary disease (mother at 50, brother at 45). His ECG shows ST elevation in the contiguous inferior leads II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL. That is an inferior STEMI. STEMI is a clinical and ECG diagnosis, and the reperfusion decision does not wait for the troponin. An early troponin may be only mildly raised, or even normal.

The focused history

Characterise the pain (site, onset, character, radiation, associated symptoms, time course, modifying factors, severity), then ask cluster questions for the other causes. Aortic dissection: sudden tearing pain to the back. Pulmonary embolism: immobility, surgery, cancer, calf pain. Pneumothorax: sudden breathlessness, pleuritic pain. Pericarditis: viral prodrome, sharp pain, better leaning forward. Heart failure: orthopnoea, PND, oedema. Oesophagitis or GORD: reflux, blood-streaked vomit, culprit medicines. Ask specifically about the cardiac risk factors (smoking, cholesterol, diabetes, hypertension, family history). Before any antithrombotic or fibrinolytic drug, check for bleeding problems, stroke, recent surgery, peptic ulcer and anticoagulant use. Before nitrates, ask about PDE5 inhibitors.

Interpreting the ECG

When time is short, state the key finding first ("ST elevation in II, III and aVF: inferior STEMI"), then work through the ECG systematically:

  1. Patient details and the date and time of the ECG
  2. Heart rate and rhythm
  3. Cardiac axis
  4. P waves
  5. PR interval
  6. QRS complex
  7. ST segments
  8. T waves
  9. U waves
  10. Documentation and comparison with previous ECGs

Which artery, and why it matters

The inferior wall is supplied by the right coronary artery in most people (right-dominant circulation), and by the left circumflex in a left-dominant circulation. ST elevation greater in III than II, with reciprocal depression in I or aVL, favours the right coronary artery. The right coronary artery usually supplies the sinoatrial and AV nodes and the right ventricle. Inferior STEMI is therefore prone to bradycardia and AV block, and to hypotension from right ventricular infarction, as James shows at 13:20. Right-sided leads (V4R) look for right ventricular involvement. Nitrates are avoided with hypotension, suspected right ventricular infarction or recent PDE5 inhibitor use, because they drop the preload these patients depend on. Symptomatic bradycardia is treated with IV atropine 500 microgram (ANZCOR; 600 microgram, one ampoule, is commonly given in Australia), repeated to a maximum of 3 mg, and, if refractory, pacing. Hypotension with a raised JVP and clear lungs suggests right ventricular infarction and responds to cautious fluid.

Acute management

  • DRSABCD, call for help, continuous monitoring and defibrillator pads.
  • Oxygen only if hypoxic. The Australian ACS guideline advises against routine oxygen when SpO2 is 93% or above.
  • Aspirin 300 mg chewed or dispersed, with a P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulation as the interventional team directs.
  • Sublingual GTN for ischaemic pain only if BP allows and right ventricular infarction is not suspected, so not for James.
  • IV access and bloods, and small, titrated IV opioid doses for severe pain (fentanyl preferred over morphine given the hypotension and bradycardia; morphine delays oral P2Y12 absorption) with an antiemetic, watching the BP.
  • Reperfusion: primary PCI if it can be done within 90 minutes of first medical contact, as here with an on-site cath lab. In a hospital without PCI, or if the cath lab is unavailable, and symptoms began less than 12 hours ago, give fibrinolysis (for example tenecteplase), ideally within 30 minutes of arrival, after checking contraindications, then transfer for angiography (pharmaco-invasive strategy).

Long-term management

Secondary prevention follows the Australian ACS guideline and the ACSQHC Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard. Medicines: aspirin long term with a P2Y12 inhibitor for 12 months, a high-intensity statin started early, a beta blocker once the bradycardia has settled (particularly if LV function is reduced on echo), and an ACE inhibitor (or ARB), indicated here for hypertension and after MI, with a plan for his amlodipine. He also needs sublingual GTN with a written action plan. Lifestyle: keep up exercise, a diet low in saturated fat, stay a non-smoker, moderate alcohol, manage stress. Everyone after ACS should be referred to cardiac rehabilitation before discharge.

Safety netting and follow-up

He needs a chest pain action plan: stop and rest, use GTN, and call 000 if the pain is severe, getting worse or lasts 10 minutes. He should also report breathlessness, fainting, palpitations, bleeding on dual antiplatelet therapy, or swelling at the access site. Follow-up covers cardiac rehabilitation, early GP review, cardiology review with an assessment of LV function, repeat lipids on treatment, driving restrictions under Austroads (private drivers do not drive for 2 weeks after an MI), and a plan for returning to work. His strong family history means first-degree relatives should have a cardiovascular risk assessment with their GP.
points: STEMI is an ECG and clinical diagnosis. Activate the cath lab without waiting for the troponin, aiming for primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact.

In a hospital without PCI, or if the cath lab is unavailable, and symptoms began less than 12 hours ago, give fibrinolysis (for example tenecteplase), ideally within 30 minutes of arrival, after checking contraindications, then transfer for angiography (pharmaco-invasive strategy). Always check bleeding and stroke history.
ST elevation in II, III and aVF is an inferior STEMI, usually from the right coronary artery, which supplies the AV node and right ventricle. Expect bradycardia, AV block and hypotension.
In an inferior STEMI with hypotension, avoid nitrates, record right-sided leads (V4R) and treat with cautious fluid, atropine for symptomatic bradycardia and pacing if refractory.
Give aspirin 300 mg at once, and oxygen only if SpO2 is below 93%.

Secondary prevention: dual antiplatelet therapy for 12 months, a high-intensity statin, a beta blocker (particularly if LV function is reduced), an ACE inhibitor, a GTN action plan and cardiac rehabilitation.
